generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, the active design of learning is easy to see. A physiology practical is built around collecting and interpreting test data, not watching a demonstration. A coaching workshop has you plan and defend a session, and a sport-management seminar has you weigh a participation strategy. Tutors set these up from the intended learning outcomes, so when a session asks you to apply or evaluate, the activity is there for you to do.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport and exercise science students see the same physiology practical on their timetable, with a pre-task: read one training study and come ready to argue whether its testing protocol supports its claim.

Tom reads the study and highlights the main results to revise later. In the practical, Tom waits to be told what the data mean. The session is built around interpreting results, but Tom has prepared as if it were a lecture, so there is little to contribute. This treats an active design as a passive one.

Amara notices the pre-task is asking for a judgement, so prepares one: the claim, the protocol and sample it rests on, and a reason the testing might be questioned. In the practical, Amara joins the analysis straight away. By reading the design of the session, Amara arrived able to do the very thing it was built for.

Both students did the reading. Only Amara worked out what the session was designed to make them do, and prepared for that.
generatedProse.summary: University learning in the School of Sport is designed to be active: you learn physiology by testing and interpreting, and coaching by planning and defending a session. Most of it is constructivist, with some behaviourist, process-driven training, such as drilling a lab technique or a movement skill. Tutors design backwards from intended learning outcomes, so each activity has a purpose you can see. You can now tell active design from passive, explain constructive alignment, and work out how to engage with a sport session on its own terms. The next lesson turns to how your work is judged.

check.body: A sport and exercise science tutor sets the outcome 'by the end you will be able to evaluate a testing protocol' before planning the practical. Why decide the outcome first?

items.text: So the activities and content can be built to lead you to that outcome (constructive alignment).
Because the outcome is a formality recorded after the class.
So the practical can cover as many tests as possible.
Because the reading must be chosen before anyone knows its purpose.

feedback.correct: That's right. Deciding the outcome first lets the tutor align the practical's activities and reading to it, which is constructive alignment.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the outcome is for in the design of the practical.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The outcome is set first so the activities and reading can be aligned to lead you to it. This backward design is constructive alignment.
